# An atypical presentation of Pembrolizumab-induced bullous pemphigoid in a patient with uterine serous carcinoma

**Authors:** Rachel Y. Chen; Chirag Vasavda; Sotonye Imadojemu; Stephanie W. Liu; Susana M. Campos

**Affiliations:** aHarvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | bDepartment of Dermatology, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | cKrantz Family Center for Cancer Research, Massachusetts General Hospital Cancer Center, Charlestown, MA, USA | dDana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced bullous pemphigoid (ICI-BP) is a rare but recognized complication of immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Compared to conventional BP, ICI-BP can present atypically, leading to delayed diagnosis and treatment, which can devastate quality of life for cancer patients. Literature on the presentation, diagnosis, and management of ICI-BP in patients with gynecologic cancer is scarce.

We report a case of ICI-BP presenting as erythema multiforme (EM)–like lesions in a woman in her early 60s with stage IVB uterine serous carcinoma. Upon diagnosis, the patient was treated with neoadjuvant carboplatin/paclitaxel followed by debulking surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy, and maintenance pembrolizumab immunotherapy. Pembrolizumab was discontinued after four cycles due to uveitis. Two months thereafter, she acutely developed painful oral mucosal erosions and a progressive palmoplantar eruption composed of targetoid and pseudo-targetoid plaques, leading to limited mobility and oral intake. Initial clinical evaluation favored EM, for which she began empiric antivirals and high-potency topical corticosteroids. Dermatology performed a skin biopsy which supported the diagnosis of ICI-BP with concomitant EM secondary to varicella zoster reactivation. The patient improved with systemic and topical corticosteroids followed by dupilumab as maintenance therapy. She was able to taper off systemic corticosteroids without recurrence of BP in eight weeks from rash onset.

This case report exemplifies a delayed-onset, atypically presenting instance of ICI-BP in a patient with uterine serous carcinoma, and substantiates the utility of dupilumab as a steroid-sparing option for ICI-BP.

## Introduction

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) have been instrumental in the management of patients with endometrial cancer as outlined by landmark studies NRG-GY018 (Eskander et al., 2025) and RUBY (Powell et al., 2024). These studies both reported a progression-free survival benefit and most recently an overall survival advantage in patients receiving programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitor maintenance therapy (Eskander et al., 2025; Powell et al., 2024; Eskander et al., 2026).

Pembrolizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody antagonist of PD-1, a receptor expressed on T-cells, B-cells, and macrophages that induces immune tolerance and anergy. Many cancers hijack this system by upregulating surface expression of the PD-1 ligand to decrease host anti-tumor immunity. Thus, pembrolizumab decreases systemic immune tolerance against cancers, but also healthy host tissue, resulting in immune-related adverse events (irAEs). An underappreciated but prominent class of irAE are cutaneous irAEs (cirAEs), which affect 15% of patients on ICI and often precede development of noncutaneous irAEs (Thompson et al., 2021). Classic cirAEs can range from more benign morbilliform drug exanthems to severe life-threatening eruptions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and progressive immunotherapy-related mucocutaneous eruption. Additional cirAEs include psoriasiform eruptions, lichenoid eruptions, and autoimmune blistering diseases such as bullous pemphigoid (BP).

BP is a cirAE more commonly caused by anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapies such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab compared to other ICIs (Thompson et al., 2021; Asdourian et al., 2022). ICI-BP presents substantially later than most cirAEs, often as a late drug eruption with a median onset time of 22 weeks after pembrolizumab initiation (IQR of 13–51 weeks) (Asdourian et al., 2022).

Here, we present a case of pembrolizumab-induced BP in a patient with uterine serous carcinoma, subsequently successfully treated with dupilumab, an immune agent that decreases type 2 inflammation.

## Case presentation

The patient is a woman in her early 60s, diagnosed with stage IVB metastatic adenocarcinoma consistent with spread from a Mullerian primary. The immunohistochemical stains performed on cell block sections revealed the following profile in the lesional cells: positive for WT-1, AE1/AE3, PAX8, p53 (strong diffuse, mutant pattern), claudin-4 and negative for CDX2, TTF-1. The tumor was pMMR and HER2/neu negative. At the time of presentation, the primary site of her disease (ovarian versus uterine) was not known. She was initially treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. She thereafter underwent a modified radical hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Pathology reported a high-grade serous carcinoma of the endometrium. She was subsequently treated with three more cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel chemotherapy followed by four cycles of pembrolizumab maintenance therapy. Her last pembrolizumab infusion was deferred due to bilateral intermediate uveitis, which was Grade 3 per the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v6.0. The uveitis was treated with prednisolone acetate 1% eye drops.

Two months following her last pembrolizumab infusion, the patient presented to the emergency department (ED) with 5 days of rash. Initially, she noticed red pinpoint macules on the bilateral palms that matured into targetoid, confluent, and tender papules and plaques (Fig. 1A). The eruption spread proximally toward the elbows and on the plantar feet (Fig. 1C, D). Three days after onset of the eruption, painful vesicles developed on her lower lip, which subsequently ruptured and formed crusts (Fig. 1B). The lip pain prevented her from eating and drinking. She denied a history of cold sores, genital pain, and eye pain, and was fully vaccinated for shingles. Dermatology consulted, who initially felt that her targetoid mucocutaneous eruption involving the palms, soles, and lips was overall most consistent with erythema multiforme (EM). She was discharged with dexamethasone mouth wash and topical clobetasol. The patient was subsequently admitted for further evaluation and a higher level of care. Repeat VZV PCR testing of a dermal sample returned positive, prompting initiation of intravenous acyclovir. Additional infectious workups remained negative, including rapid strep antigen testing and serologies for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), HSV, and mycoplasma pneumoniae.

Given her progressive debilitating eruption, additional workups were pursued, including skin biopsies and serologies for autoimmune blistering disorders (Fig. 2D). Biopsies revealed subepidermal blisters with a prominent eosinophilic infiltrate, with direct immunofluorescence (DIF) studies identifying linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane. Serologies against collagen XII (also known as BP antigen 180, [BP180 or BPAG2]) and BP Antigen 230 [BP230 or BPAG1] autoantibodies revealed positive titers against BP180/BPAG2 (21 RU/mL, reference range < 20R U/mL). Together, the biopsies, serologies, and clinical presentation suggested a diagnosis of Grade 3 BP per CTCAE v6.0, likely as a cirAE from pembrolizumab. However, the differential included concomitant Grade 3 EM secondary to VZV given her positive VZV PCR testing, though the positive DIF and serologies could not be explained by EM alone.

Her diagnosis of ICI-BP prompted initiation of a systemic methylprednisolone taper from 1 mg/kg/day alongside intravenous acyclovir. She was discharged with oral valacyclovir, a two-month prednisone taper, and was prescribed topical steroids for adjunctive local relief. After a week of multimodal therapy, her pain improved to the point where she could walk again.

One month after discharge, the patient received her first dose of dupilumab followed by maintenance doses every other week. With just one month of dupilumab therapy, she was able to discontinue topical and systemic steroids and return to full-time work. After 28 weeks on dupilumab, the dosing interval was extended to once every three weeks, with the goal of discontinuing dupilumab afterward. She has not experienced recurrence of BP.

## Discussion

Pembrolizumab, a highly selective anti-PD-1 IgG4 antibody, has been used to treat a variety of cancers including melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, Hodgkin's lymphoma, breast cancer, urothelial cancer, cervical cancer, and advanced endometrial cancer. It has been used alone and in combination with standard chemotherapy for over a decade. Pembrolizumab functions by inhibiting the PD-1 immune checkpoint. In typical physiology, T-cells, B-cells, and macrophages expressing PD-1 bind to the PD-L1 ligand on target cells to mediate self-tolerance and prevent autoimmunity. However, some cancers exploit this mechanism by expressing membrane PD-L1 to evade immune surveillance. Inhibition of PD-1 signaling by pembrolizumab activates the immune system against such cancers, but in many patients induces immune overactivation resembling auto-immune disease. These irAEs may involve any system or organ, most commonly the skin (associated with mild pruritus, maculopapular rash, lichenoid dermatitis, psoriasis, and vitiligo), gastrointestinal system (colitis and diarrhea), and thyroid (Thompson et al., 2021). The incidence of hospitalization with irAEs after ICI therapy has been reported at 15% (Durbin et al., 2025).

Cutaneous irAEs (cirAEs) occur in approximately 20% of patients within two years of ICI initiation (Zhang et al., 2023). BP, a severe and potentially debilitating condition, has been reported to constitute 2% of cirAEs (Thompson et al., 2021). Patients with pembrolizumab-associated BP typically present with tense bullae and blisters, pruritus, and erythema on the limbs and trunk, with median time to bulla formation of 22 weeks after drug initiation (Asdourian et al., 2022). ICI-driven pathophysiology often causes atypical presentations of BP. Accordingly, our patient presented with a prominent blistering palmoplantar eruption, pseudo-targetoid and true-targetoid papules, dusky palpable flaccid vesicles in deep violaceous plaques, and buccal mucosal involvement. Onset was four months after the first infusion of pembrolizumab and two months after its discontinuation. The initial diagnosis of EM was empiric, owing to the targetoid appearance of the eruption. Immunofluorescence staining of a punch biopsy led to the diagnosis of BP, as it was positive for BP230 and BP180 autoantibodies and C3 along the basement membrane. It is difficult to delineate whether the appearance of targetoid papules was due to VZV, mycoplasma pneumoniae-induced EM, and/or atypical presentation of BP.

A proposed mechanism for ICI-BP is the overactivation of autoreactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Th2 CD4+ cells increase B-cell antibody production against cutaneous antigens such as BP180 and BP230 via the interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13 axis. This triggers inflammation, complement activation, and immune cell infiltration, leading to ICI-BP (Yin et al., 2023). ICI-BP patients require significantly higher daily doses of corticosteroids during the first six months of treatment compared to conventional BP (Saffuri et al., 2025). Many cases of ICI-BP are also corticosteroid resistant and persist for months after discontinuation of ICI therapy, unlike conventional BP (Asdourian et al., 2022). Therefore, providers of patients on or recently off ICIs should have a low threshold for early dermatology referral, pursue detailed diagnostic investigations including biopsies, and treat vigorously.

Pembrolizumab-induced BP is conventionally treated with immunosuppressants such as systemic and topical steroids in combination with doxycycline, niacinamide, dapsone, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, or rituximab. Depending on BP severity and treatment response, pembrolizumab is often held or discontinued. However, immunosuppressants limit the immune-potentiating effect of pembrolizumab against tumor cells and may compromise cancer management. Accordingly, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network released guidelines recommending dupilumab as a steroid-sparing measure against severe ICI-BP in January 2026 (Schneider et al., 2026).

Dupilumab is an immune modulating agent that blocks IL-4 receptor α, the shared subunit in receptors of IL-4 and IL-13. IL-4 and IL-13 produced by skin-homing T cells are elevated in skin lesions of both conventional BP and ICI-BP (Shipman et al., 2023). Several studies have reported achieving partial or complete remission of conventional and ICI-BP with dupilumab without increasing adverse events, infection rates, or mortality (Khattab et al., 2025; Nykaza et al., 2025). In fact, patients with cirAEs treated with dupilumab have had significantly better survival outcomes compared to those treated with systemic glucocorticoids without dupilumab (Khattab et al., 2025). Another study showed that 62% of patients with ICI-BP achieved complete response with dupilumab as the only active systemic agent, with a median time to first response of 19.5 days. Over half of these patients had previously failed oral corticosteroid therapy (Nykaza et al., 2025). Thus, dupilumab presents an efficacious alternative to high-dose corticosteroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, and rituximab, all of which dampen antitumor immunity and the efficacy of ICI. Dupilumab has even allowed for continued administration or recontinuation of the provoking ICI after ICI-BP (Shipman et al., 2023; Nykaza et al., 2025).

More broadly, dupilumab treatment for patients with conventional BP reduced systemic steroid use by 82% at week 52 with few adverse events (Planella-Fontanillas et al., 2025). Patients receiving dupilumab with methylprednisolone and azathioprine also required a significantly shorter steroid taper and lower cumulative steroid dose than patients not receiving dupilumab (Zhang et al., 2021). Our report adds to the limited evidence showing that dupilumab is an efficacious and safe steroid-sparing agent for the treatment of ICI-BP, not just conventional BP.

Our patient was treated with systemic and topical steroids during the acute phase of her hospitalization, before a definitive diagnosis of BP. She was discharged on moderate dose prednisone, which controlled inflammation and provided a bridge to dupilumab. Within one month of starting dupilumab, she was able to taper off prednisone. As of writing, she has been off prednisone for nine months and has lengthened the dosing interval of dupilumab to once every three weeks, with plans to stop completely. She is continuing prophylactic valacyclovir indefinitely. There has been no recurrence of cutaneous symptoms, although it is difficult to delimit the contribution of dupilumab versus time from pembrolizumab discontinuation in the resolution of her ICI-BP.

Despite our patient's successful recovery from the pembrolizumab-induced uveitis, bullous dermatosis, and erythema multiforme-like eruptions, these Grade 3 events per CTCAE v6.0 were debilitating, painful, and disrupted her life. It is important to report on these rare, yet significant, adverse events. In addition, emerging data from the NRG-GY018 demonstrated an overall survival benefit to IO therapy [dMMR HR 0.53 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.89), pMMR HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.06)]0.3 Thus, in the era of immune-oncology for endometrial cancers, early recognition and timely evaluation of rare adverse events can prevent complications and ensure that appropriate treatment is provided promptly.

## Conclusion

We present an atypical case of ICI-BP in a patient in her early 60s with uterine serous carcinoma treated with pembrolizumab. She was managed acutely with systemic and topical corticosteroids followed by steroid-sparing dupilumab. BP is an established complication of pembrolizumab, and in this case, diagnosis was complicated by an atypical EM-like presentation and positive VZV testing. ICI-BP causes debilitating pain, pruritus, and discomfort, and thus should remain on the differential even months after initiation or discontinuation of pembrolizumab. Dupilumab may be considered as a management option that has less interference with patients' anti-tumor immunity and ICI therapy. It is critical to encourage patients to report any unexpected or severe symptoms without delay, even if they seem unrelated to ICI treatment. Early mitigation of ICI toxicity reduces the risk of debilitating complications and may potentially enable patients to remain on treatment.
